title: Google Is Spending $15 Billion on a Data Center in Vizag. The City Gets One Hour of Tap Water a Day.
excerpt: Andhra Pradesh is offering $2.3 billion in subsidies — discounted water, discounted land, tax waivers — to a company worth $2 trillion. Farmers who grew mangoes for 50 years are being pushed out. A Wall Street Journal investigation reveals the costs of India's AI ambitions.
body:
When Google broke ground in late April on what will be India's first hub for training and running large-scale AI models, the Andhra Pradesh government celebrated it as a transformative moment for Visakhapatnam — the sleepy coastal city of two million affectionately known as Vizag.

Some residents had never heard of AI.

What they know is that Vizag does not have much water. Some areas receive less than one hour of tap water per day. The World Resources Institute classifies the city as under "extremely high" water stress. And now, according to a Wall Street Journal investigation published this week, the state government is offering Google roughly $2.3 billion in subsidies over 20 years — including a 25 percent discount on water — to build a facility that, when running at full capacity, will consume the equivalent electricity of six million Indians per year.

The Subsidies

The incentive package is staggering for a state with limited fiscal room. According to state government documents obtained by the Journal, Andhra Pradesh is providing Google:

A 25 percent discount on water costs for 10 years. A 25 percent discount on land. Reimbursement of electricity infrastructure and upgrade costs. Waivers on state taxes. Discounts on power costs.

Google is working on the project with Bharti Airtel and Adani Group. The hub will eventually span three sites across at least 600 acres — roughly 454 football fields — making it one of the largest data-center complexes in South Asia.

The Farmers

For Pyla Kondamma, a 42-year-old farmer who has grown mangoes and cashews for decades on government-owned land, the Google announcement meant eviction. The state offered her roughly $83,000 in compensation. Many residents will receive a smaller plot elsewhere.

"How can we be happy about Google coming?" she told the Journal. "We'll all be scattered. It feels very sad."

Bali Venkata Raju, another farmer, received roughly $115,000 to leave land he had farmed for 40 years. "The government can evict you from what you thought was yours for so long," he said. "There are no legal rights to fight over it."

Rights groups have criticized the lack of public consultation about the project's environmental impact. V.S. Krishna of the Human Rights Forum called it "a very, very troubling convergence of corporate power and full-state patronage."

The Water Math

Data centers typically require vast amounts of water for cooling. Google says its Vizag facility will initially operate primarily with air cooling — a setup that uses far less water than evaporative systems — and has committed to powering the project with 100 percent renewable energy, undersea telecom cables connecting Vizag to the rest of Asia, and programs to replenish more freshwater than it consumes globally by 2030.

The company is also planning GPS navigation tools for local fishermen and AI training programs for students.

Critics say those pledges are superficial. The fundamental tension — a $2 trillion company receiving public subsidies in a city where residents queue for an hour of tap water — remains unresolved.

The Bigger Picture

India is not alone in wrestling with this dilemma. Malaysia, Thailand, Kenya, and the Philippines are all experiencing data-center build-outs growing 20 to 40 percent annually, faster than in the United States, according to Structure Research. Protests have erupted in Johor Bahru and Batam over risks to water and power supplies.

But India's stakes are uniquely high. Morgan Stanley forecasts Indian data-center capacity will grow fivefold to roughly 10 gigawatts over the next five years. Microsoft faces allegations in an Indian court of illegally occupying public land near Hyderabad for a data center. Amazon has faced similar farmer displacement complaints nearby.

Driving the urgency is a fear among Indian officials that the world's most populous country could become collateral damage in the AI race. Indian IT services firms saw tens of billions wiped off their market values this year over fears that AI could replace the software and labor they export. India needs to become an AI consumer and builder, not just a provider of the humans being automated away.

Anthropic opened an office in Bengaluru in February, noting India is the second-largest market globally for Claude. OpenAI's ChatGPT has 100 million weekly users in the country.

The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs working in Big Tech — many of whom helped build the AI systems now being deployed back in India — the Vizag story raises uncomfortable questions about the terms on which their employers are investing in their home country. The data-center boom is creating high-value jobs and positioning India in the global AI supply chain. But it is also displacing communities, straining resources, and raising the same environmental justice concerns that have stalled projects in the American heartland.

The difference is that in Vizag, some of the displaced did not know what AI was. They just knew they were losing their farms.
